noteBlocks.caption: One gene, two alleles, one on each chromosome of the pair. The dominant one decides the coat.

noteBlocks.md: A **gene** controls a characteristic, and it comes in versions called **alleles**. Chromosomes come in pairs, so a body cell carries **two alleles** of each gene, one from each parent. In guinea pigs the allele **R** gives a rough coat and **r** a smooth one.

A **dominant** allele shows whenever it is present; a **recessive** allele shows only when both alleles are recessive. The **genotype** is the pair of letters: RR, Rr or rr. The **phenotype** is what you see: rough or smooth. Two alleles the same is **homozygous**; two different is **heterozygous**.

steps.working: Phenotype: a rough coat.
steps.decision: R is dominant, so one R is enough for it to show.

noteBlocks.prompt: In maize, the allele P for purple kernels is dominant to p for yellow kernels. A maize plant is pp. What is its phenotype?
options: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
noteBlocks.explain: A recessive allele shows only when both alleles are recessive, and pp has no P to hide it, so the kernels are yellow. In the See it, Rr was rough because one dominant allele is enough.

optionNotes.why: Purple needs at least one P, the dominant allele, and this plant has none.

optionNotes.option: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
optionNotes.why: A blend would mean neither allele is dominant; here P is dominant, and with two p the kernels are simply yellow.

twin.prompt: In maize, P (purple kernels) is dominant to p (yellow kernels). A maize plant is Pp. What is its phenotype?
options: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
twin.explain: One P is enough to show, because P is dominant: a Pp plant has purple kernels.

optionNotes.why: Yellow needs two recessive alleles; the single P is dominant and shows.

optionNotes.option: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
optionNotes.why: A dominant allele hides the recessive one completely, so there is no blend of the two colours.

noteBlocks.md: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two chromosomes of a pair. **Meiosis** puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete, so a gamete carries **one** allele of each gene, never two. An Rr guinea pig makes R gametes and r gametes in equal numbers.

noteBlocks.title: Why a Punnett square works
noteBlocks.md: At fertilisation two gametes fuse, so the zygote has **two** alleles again, and mitosis copies both into every body cell. Which sperm meets which egg is down to **chance**, so every pairing of gametes is equally likely. A Punnett square's four boxes are those pairings.

noteBlocks.stem: A guinea pig has the genotype Rr. Give the alleles its gametes can carry, and explain why each gamete carries only one. [2]

steps.working: Its gametes carry R or r, half of each.
steps.decision: One letter for each gamete. A gamete written as Rr loses the mark: it carries one allele.

steps.working: Meiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete.
steps.decision: The two alleles are on the two chromosomes of a pair, so they go to different gametes.

noteBlocks.prompt: In sheep, W (white wool) is dominant to w (black wool). A sheep is Ww. Which describes its gametes?
options: half carry W and half carry w
half carry WW and half carry ww
noteBlocks.answer: half carry W and half carry w
noteBlocks.explain: Meiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete, so each gamete gets one allele: W or w, in equal numbers. The Rr guinea pig in the See it made R and r gametes the same way.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because Ww is the sheep's genotype, but a gamete carries only one allele of the pair.

optionNotes.option: half carry WW and half carry ww
optionNotes.why: Two letters is a genotype; gametes carry one allele each, so W or w, never a pair.

twin.prompt: A maize plant has the genotype PP. Which describes its gametes?
options: half carry P and half carry p
twin.explain: A PP plant has two P alleles, so whichever chromosome a gamete gets, it carries P.

optionNotes.option: half carry P and half carry p
optionNotes.why: That is a Pp plant's gametes; this plant has no p to pass on.
A gamete carries one allele, not a pair: P on its own.

Write each genotype with the capital letter first (Rr, never rR), then give each box its phenotype. CCEA's marks go to the square, to each parent's gametes, and to the cross being right.

noteBlocks.stem: Two guinea pigs, Rr and rr, are crossed. Show their offspring's possible genotypes in a Punnett square. [4]

steps.working: Draw a square of four boxes.
steps.decision: The square earns its own mark before any letters go in.

steps.working: Across the top, the Rr parent's gametes: R and r.
steps.decision: One allele per box: the parent's two alleles split.

steps.working: Down the side, the rr parent's gametes: r and r.
steps.decision: A homozygous parent still makes two gametes, both the same.

steps.working: Fill the boxes: Rr, rr, Rr, rr.
steps.decision: Each box takes the letter above and the letter beside it; capital first.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two maize plants, both Pp, are crossed. Which genotypes do their offspring have, box by box?
noteBlocks.explain: Each parent gives P or p, so P and p go across the top and down the side. The boxes are then PP, Pp, Pp and pp. The See it filled Rr × rr the same way.

optionNotes.why: Every box Pp would need one parent to give only P and the other only p; both parents here make P and p gametes.
It pairs P with P and p with p only; each box takes one letter from the top and one from the side.

twin.prompt: Two guinea pigs, RR and rr, are crossed. Which genotypes do their pups have, box by box?
twin.explain: The RR parent gives only R and the rr parent only r, so every box is Rr.

optionNotes.why: That is the square for two Rr parents; here each parent makes only one kind of gamete.
Each box takes one letter from each parent, so it can never be RR or rr here.

noteBlocks.md: Each parent passes on either allele with an equal chance, a half. An rr pup needs r from **both** Rr parents: a half times a half, **¼**. RR is also ¼, and Rr is **½**, because it can happen two ways.
So two heterozygous parents give genotypes **1 : 2 : 1** and phenotypes **3 : 1**, because RR and Rr look alike. A heterozygous parent crossed with a homozygous recessive one gives **1 : 1**.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that a cross between two heterozygous guinea pigs gives rough and smooth offspring in the ratio 3 : 1. [3]

steps.working: Each parent gives R or r, each with a chance of ½.
steps.decision: Meiosis puts each allele into half the gametes.

steps.working: rr: ½ × ½ = ¼. RR: ¼. Rr: ¼ + ¼ = ½.
steps.decision: Rr arises two ways: R from the father or R from the mother.

steps.working: Rough (RR or Rr): ¼ + ½ = ¾. Smooth: ¼. So 3 : 1.
steps.decision: Three quarters to one quarter is three to one.

noteBlocks.explain: Pp arises two ways, P from either parent, so it is ½ of the offspring: 2 out of every 4. The See it found Rr a half for two Rr guinea pigs.

twin.prompt: Two maize plants, both Pp, are crossed. Out of every 4 offspring, how many are expected to have purple kernels?
twin.explain: Purple is PP or Pp: ¼ + ½ = ¾, so 3 out of every 4.

noteBlocks.md: The square gives four boxes; the question decides the form. **Ratio**: the numbers in the order the question names the phenotypes. **Percentage**: boxes out of 4, times 100. **Probability**: 1 in 4, ¼ or 0.25. **Expected number**: the fraction times the number of offspring.

Real counts rarely match the expected number exactly, because fertilisation is random. Two traps cost marks: a ratio written backwards, and a genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) given where a phenotype ratio was asked.

noteBlocks.stem: In cats, short hair (S) is dominant to long hair (s). An Ss cat and an ss cat have 36 kittens. How many are expected to have long hair? [2]

steps.working: Square: Ss, ss, Ss, ss. Long hair is ss: 2 boxes in 4, a half.
steps.decision: Fill the square first, then count the boxes the question is about.

steps.working: 36 × ½ = 18 kittens.
steps.decision: The fraction times the number of offspring. The real count may differ a little, by chance.

noteBlocks.md: A late question of seven to eleven marks, opened by a pedigree or a described cross. The first mark is usually a genotype or a term; the last is a ratio, a percentage or a test cross described in full. Stuck? Write each parent's genotype, split it into gametes, and draw the square.

workedExamples.stem: In tomato plants, red fruit (R) is dominant to yellow fruit (r). A homozygous red-fruited plant is crossed with a yellow-fruited plant, and two plants of the first generation are then crossed. Complete the diagram: the parents' genotypes and gametes, the first generation, its gametes and the second generation. [4]

steps.working: Parents RR and rr; gametes R and r.
steps.decision: Homozygous red is RR; yellow, the recessive phenotype, can only be rr. Each makes one kind of gamete.

steps.working: First generation: Rr and Rr.
steps.decision: Every plant takes R from one parent and r from the other, so all are red.

steps.working: Gametes of each first-generation plant: R and r.
steps.decision: Each first-generation plant is heterozygous, so half its gametes carry R and half r.

steps.working: Second generation: RR, Rr, Rr, rr.
steps.decision: Three red to one yellow: yellow reappears because two r gametes can meet.

options: Because two Rr parents can each pass on r
Because yellow is dominant in the second generation
Because the first generation plants were rr
whyMenu.explain: Both first-generation plants carry a hidden r. When an r gamete from each meets, the offspring is rr and has yellow fruit.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: RR and rr; R and r; Rr and Rr; R and r from each; RR, Rr, Rr, rr.

twin.stem: In the same two-generation tomato cross, what fraction of the second generation is heterozygous?

options.feedback: Rr fills two boxes of four: one half.
One in four is RR or rr; Rr happens two ways, so it is two boxes in four.
Three in four is the red phenotype, RR and Rr together; heterozygous is Rr only.

workedExamples.stem: In fruit flies, normal wings (N) are dominant to vestigial wings (n). A breeder has a fly with normal wings and does not know its genotype. Show, with two Punnett squares, the test (back) crosses that would find its genotype. [4]

steps.working: Two squares, because the fly could be NN or Nn.
steps.decision: A normal-winged fly shows the dominant phenotype, so either genotype is possible.

steps.working: Cross each with a vestigial-winged fly, nn: n and n down the side of both squares.
steps.decision: A homozygous recessive partner passes on only n, so every offspring shows the allele the unknown gave.

options: Because nn passes on only the recessive allele
Because nn flies have the most offspring
Because the partner must match the unknown fly
whyMenu.explain: Every offspring gets n from the partner, so whether it has normal or vestigial wings depends only on the allele from the unknown fly.

steps.working: NN × nn: Nn, Nn, Nn, Nn, so every offspring has normal wings.
steps.decision: An NN parent gives only N.

steps.working: Nn × nn: Nn, nn, Nn, nn, so about half have vestigial wings.
steps.decision: Any vestigial offspring proves the unknown fly is Nn.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Two squares, both with an nn partner: NN × nn gives all Nn; Nn × nn gives Nn, nn, Nn, nn.

twin.stem: The breeder's test cross gives 38 flies with normal wings and 41 with vestigial wings. What was the unknown fly's genotype?

options.feedback: Vestigial offspring are nn and took n from the unknown fly, so it is Nn; about half and half fits Nn × nn.
An NN fly gives only N, so every offspring would have normal wings.
An nn fly has vestigial wings itself; the unknown fly has normal wings.

steps.working: Individual 6 has albinism: aa.
steps.decision: Shaded is the recessive phenotype here, so it has only one genotype.

steps.working: 6 took an a from each parent; 4 has normal skin, so 4 is Aa.
steps.decision: One allele from each parent: 4 has an a to give and an A to show.

options: Because her son has albinism and she does not
Because she married into the family
Because her daughter 7 has normal skin
whyMenu.explain: Her son 6 is aa, so he took an a from her; she has normal skin, so her other allele is A. A normal daughter tells you nothing extra.

steps.working: 3 is Aa (his mother, 2, has albinism): Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa, aa, so the probability is 1 in 4.
steps.decision: Fix both parents before the square; each child is a fresh one-in-four chance.

twin.stem: On the same pedigree, what can be said about the genotype of individual 1?

options.text: AA or Aa: the pedigree cannot tell which
options.feedback: 1 has normal skin, and his children with 2 all have normal skin, so nothing shows whether he carries a.

options.text: Aa, because his partner has albinism
options.feedback: His partner's genotype says nothing about his; none of his children has albinism.
aa would give him albinism; he has normal skin.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from earlier topics. What is an allele?

options.text: a different form of the same gene
options.feedback: A different version of one gene, sitting at the same place on a pair of chromosomes.

options.text: a short length of DNA that controls a characteristic
options.feedback: That is a gene. An allele is one of its versions.

options.text: all of the genetic material of an organism
options.feedback: That is the genome.

options.text: a structure in the nucleus made of DNA
options.feedback: That is a chromosome.

items.stem: How many chromosomes of each pair does a gamete carry?
items.skill: Recall what meiosis does to a pair

options.feedback: One of each pair, which is why a gamete carries one allele of each gene.
Two would be the body cell's number; meiosis halves it.
Four is the number of cells meiosis makes, not the number of chromosomes per pair.
A gamete carries a full single set, one of every pair.

items.stem: 3 of the 4 boxes in a square show one outcome. What percentage is that?
items.skill: Turn a count into a percentage

options.feedback: 3 ÷ 4 × 100 = 75. The same move ends almost every question in this topic.
That is the box left over, not the boxes that show the outcome.
The division is right, but it gives a proportion. Multiply by 100 to turn it into a percentage.
That is the number of boxes, not the percentage.

items.stem: Which word describes a genotype whose two alleles are different?

options.feedback: Hetero means different.
Homo means the same, so that is a genotype whose alleles match.
Dominant describes an allele, not a pair of them.
The phenotype is what you can see.

items.stem: A Shetland pony has the genotype BB, where B is dominant. Which term describes it?

options.feedback: Both alleles the same, and both dominant.
That is bb, where both alleles are the recessive one.
There is no such term: heterozygous already means one of each.
That describes what it looks like, not its pair of alleles.

items.stem: A Bb parent makes gametes. What does each gamete carry?

options.text: one allele, either B or b
options.feedback: One allele each, because meiosis takes one of every pair.
A gamete written as a pair is the commonest slip in this topic.

options.text: two alleles the same, BB or bb
options.feedback: That is a genotype, not a gamete.
A gamete carries a full single set of alleles, one per gene.

items.stem: Two Bb parents are crossed. Which set of genotypes fills the four boxes of the Punnett square?

options.text: one BB, two Bb and one bb
options.feedback: B with B gives BB, B with b gives Bb, and b with b gives bb.
That would need every pairing to be one of each, which the gametes make impossible.

options.text: two BB and two bb, with no heterozygous box
options.feedback: That pairs each parent with itself instead of across the square.

options.text: B, b, B, b, the gametes copied into the boxes
options.feedback: Those are the gametes copied into the boxes.

items.stem: A Bb × Bb cross gives what phenotype ratio, black to chestnut?
items.skill: Give a phenotype ratio the right way round

options.feedback: 3 boxes show the dominant coat and 1 shows the recessive one.
That is the same ratio written backwards, and the order follows the question.
That is the genotype ratio, which counts BB and Bb apart.
An even split is what a cross with a homozygous recessive parent gives, not this one.

items.stem: In the same cross, what percentage of the offspring are expected to be chestnut?
items.skill: Turn a ratio into a percentage

options.feedback: One box in four, so 25%.
That is the percentage with the dominant phenotype.
That counts the two heterozygous boxes, which show the dominant coat.
That reads 3 : 1 as one in three; the two numbers add to four.

items.stem: In a test cross, what genotype must the partner have?

options.feedback: Only then is the partner's contribution certain, so the offspring reveal the unknown parent.
Its dominant allele would hide whatever the unknown parent gave.
That leaves two unknowns instead of one.

options.text: the same as the unknown parent
options.feedback: The whole point is that the unknown parent's genotype is not known.

items.stem: On a pedigree diagram, an individual showing the recessive phenotype must have which genotype?
items.skill: Read a pedigree from the shaded symbols

options.feedback: The recessive phenotype needs both alleles to be recessive, so it is the one certain reading on the diagram.
A heterozygous individual carries a dominant allele, so it shows the dominant phenotype.
That shows the dominant phenotype.
Only one of those two shows the recessive phenotype.

context.setting: The words a genetics question is written in

parts.stem: What is meant by the genotype of an organism?

accepted: the genotype is the alleles it carries for a characteristic
the two alleles it has for a gene

any: alleles an organism has|alleles the organism has|alleles it has for

scheme.for: the alleles present for a characteristic

hints: One of the two words is about the letters, the other about the animal.
parts.workedSolution: The genotype is the alleles it carries for a characteristic.

pattern.regex: \bwhat it looks like\b|\bappearance\b|\bwhat you can see\b|\bobservable\b

commonErrors.feedback: That describes the phenotype. The genotype is the pair of alleles behind it, which you cannot see.

parts.stem: What is meant by the phenotype of an organism?

accepted: the phenotype is the characteristic you can see

any: characteristic that is shown|characteristics that are shown|characteristic shown|characteristics shown|visible characteristic|visible characteristics

hints: The one you could judge by looking at the animal.
parts.workedSolution: The phenotype is the characteristic you can see.

parts.stem:
In Shetland ponies, the allele B gives a black coat and the allele b gives a chestnut coat.
Which genotype is heterozygous?
Circle the correct answer.

options.text: Bb (one dominant allele and one recessive allele)
options.feedback: Bb: two different alleles, which is what heterozygous means.
BB is homozygous dominant: two alleles the same, both dominant.
bb is homozygous recessive: two alleles the same, both recessive.

options.text: B (a single allele, not a pair)
options.feedback: One letter is a single allele, not a genotype. A genotype is always a pair.

hints: Hetero means different.
parts.workedSolution: Bb.

context.setting: Naming a genotype from its letters

parts.stem:
A Shetland pony has the genotype BB.
Give the term that describes this genotype.

scheme.examinerNote: The Summer 2025 Foundation report notes that surprisingly few candidates could give these two terms, so both words are needed: homozygous, and which kind.

hints: Two words: one about whether the alleles match, one about which allele it is.
parts.workedSolution: Homozygous dominant.

commonErrors.feedback: Homozygous means the two alleles match, and here they are both the dominant allele, so the term is homozygous dominant.

parts.stem:
A Shetland pony has the genotype bb.
Give the term that describes this genotype.
hints: The alleles still match, but they are the other kind.
parts.workedSolution: Homozygous recessive.

commonErrors.feedback: Both alleles are the recessive one here, so the term is homozygous recessive.

parts.stem: Give the term that describes a genotype with one dominant allele and one recessive allele.
hints: One word this time.
parts.workedSolution: Heterozygous.

parts.stem:
A Shetland pony has the genotype Bb.
Give the alleles that its gametes can carry.

scheme.for: B and b, as two separate alleles
scheme.examinerNote: The Summer 2024 Foundation report found that fewer candidates could give the alleles than the genotypes. A gamete carries one allele, so the answer is two letters written apart.

hints: A gamete is made by meiosis, so it carries one of each pair.
parts.workedSolution: B and b, written as two separate alleles.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the genotype written out again. A gamete carries only one allele of the pair, so the two letters have to be written apart.

parts.stem:
A second Shetland pony has the genotype BB.
Which alleles can its gametes carry?
Circle the correct answer.

options.text: B and B (both gametes carry the dominant allele)
options.feedback: Both alleles are the same, so every gamete carries B.

options.text: B and b (one gamete of each kind)
options.feedback: A BB parent has no b allele to pass on.

options.text: b and b (both gametes carry the recessive allele)
options.feedback: That is the gamete of a bb parent, not a BB one.

options.text: Bb (the whole pair in one gamete)
options.feedback: A gamete carries one allele, not the pair.

hints: What is there to choose between?
parts.workedSolution: B and B: a homozygous parent can only pass on the one allele it has.

In budgerigars the allele G gives green feathers and the allele g gives blue feathers.

the two gg offspring are blue

context.setting: What the offspring of a test cross prove

context.setting: Explaining a whole cross from first principles

parts.stem:
Two black Shetland ponies are bred together and one of their foals is chestnut.
Explain how two black parents can have a chestnut foal, and describe how a breeder could use a test cross to find the genotype of a black pony.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: a dominant allele shows whenever it is present, so both BB and Bb give the dominant phenotype
both parents must therefore be heterozygous, carrying one dominant and one recessive allele
each parent's gametes carry one allele, so each can pass on either the dominant or the recessive one
a foal that receives the recessive allele from both parents is homozygous recessive and shows the chestnut coat
about 25% of the foals of such a cross are expected to show the recessive phenotype, a ratio of 3 : 1
a test cross means crossing the unknown animal with a homozygous recessive one
any offspring showing the recessive phenotype proves the unknown parent is heterozygous, while all-dominant offspring point to homozygous dominant

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Two things cap an answer here. The first is a gamete written as a pair of letters: a gamete carries one allele, and an answer that gives both loses the point about gametes and usually the one after it. The second is the test cross described with the wrong partner; only a homozygous recessive partner makes the result readable. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Work in the order the marks come: what dominant means, what the parents must be, what their gametes carry, what the foal received.
Then change subject cleanly to the test cross and give both possible results.
parts.workedSolution: A dominant allele shows in the phenotype whenever it is present, so a black pony can be either BB or Bb. Since one of the foals is chestnut, and the chestnut coat only appears when both alleles are recessive, that foal must be bb. It received one recessive allele from each parent, so both parents must be heterozygous, carrying one dominant and one recessive allele. Each parent's gametes carry one allele, so each parent can pass on either the dominant or the recessive one. A foal that receives the recessive allele from both parents is homozygous recessive and shows the chestnut coat, and about 25% of the foals of such a cross are expected to be chestnut, a ratio of 3 : 1. To find the genotype of a black pony, a breeder carries out a test cross: the unknown animal is crossed with a chestnut one, which must be homozygous recessive. Any offspring showing the recessive phenotype proves the unknown parent is heterozygous, while all the offspring showing the dominant phenotype points to homozygous dominant.

commonErrors.feedback: A gamete carries one allele, not the pair. Splitting the genotype into single letters is the step that makes the rest of the cross work.

findTheMistake.stem:
Órla is asked: 'Two black ponies, both Bb, are crossed. Give the percentage of foals expected to be chestnut. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: all the foals are Bb, so 0% are chestnut
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 reads the parents correctly and earns its mark. Line 2 writes each gamete as a pair of letters. A gamete is made by meiosis, which takes one chromosome of each pair, so it carries one allele: B or b, never Bb. Because line 2 is wrong, line 3 follows it into a wrong answer.
correction: gametes: B and b from each parent
square: BB, Bb, Bb, bb, so 1 in 4 is bb, which is 25%
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the three. A quick check catches it: if every foal were Bb, no chestnut pony could ever be born from black parents, and the question says one was.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'A black pony and a chestnut pony have a chestnut foal. What percentage of their foals would you expect to be black? [3]'
His working:
studentWorking: the black parent is BB and the chestnut parent is bb
the square gives Bb, Bb, Bb, Bb
so 100% of the foals are black
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 skips the one clue the question gives. The chestnut foal is bb, so it received a recessive allele from each parent, and the black parent must therefore be Bb, not BB. Lines 2 and 3 follow correctly from line 1, which is why the answer runs on to the wrong percentage.
correction: the chestnut foal is bb, so the black parent is Bb and the chestnut parent is bb
the square gives Bb, Bb, bb, bb
so 50% of the foals are expected to be black
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the three, for a square drawn correctly from his own parents. The clue he skipped is the chestnut foal: an offspring showing the recessive phenotype tells you that both of its parents carry the recessive allele.

findTheMistake.stem:
Méabh is asked: 'Describe how a breeder could carry out a test cross on a black Shetland pony. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: cross the black pony with another black pony
if any chestnut foals appear, the unknown parent is heterozygous
if all the foals are black, the unknown parent is homozygous dominant
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The partner is wrong, and it takes the rest of the answer with it. Another black pony could itself be BB or Bb, so an all-black litter would prove nothing. The partner must be chestnut, because that phenotype can only be bb.
correction: cross the black pony with a chestnut pony, which must be bb
if any chestnut foals appear, the unknown parent is heterozygous
if all the foals are black, the unknown parent is homozygous dominant
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three: the two outcome lines are the points a scheme credits on their own. The missing mark is the partner, and it is the one that makes the test work: with a black partner an all-black litter proves nothing, because the partner itself might be BB.

prompts.prompt: Give the three terms for the genotypes BB, bb and Bb, where B is dominant.
prompts.answer: BB is homozygous dominant, bb is homozygous recessive and Bb is heterozygous.

prompts.prompt: Give the four steps of working out a cross, in order.
prompts.answer: Parents' genotypes, then gametes, then the offspring in the square, then count what the question asks for.

prompts.prompt: On a pedigree diagram, which individuals give you a certain genotype straight away?
prompts.answer: The ones showing the recessive phenotype: they must be homozygous recessive.

prompts.prompt: In tomato plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t). Two Tt plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short?
prompts.answer: One quarter, because only tt gives a short plant and one box in four is tt.

prompts.prompt: A question's part (b) names its own two parents. What must you do with the genotypes from part (a)?
prompts.answer: Leave them behind. Each part names the animals it is about, and carrying the earlier pair over loses the mark.

prompts.prompt: What genotype must the partner in a test cross have?
How many alleles of a gene does a gamete carry?
What phenotype ratio do two heterozygous parents give?

findings.asked: A pedigree and a cross: name the relationship, give genotypes, then cross a specified (bold) individual.
findings.wentWrong: The relationship had to be exact ('father', not 'parent'); many read past the bold word 'complete' and named the condition without the sex; and the Punnett square - examined many times - was still often wrong, though a correct cross from wrong gametes earned error-carried-forward marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Read the bold words twice, wrote the parental genotypes, then the gametes, then the square.
findings.rule: Bold words in a genetics stem are the whole question; genotypes before gametes before square.

findings.asked: A cross over two generations from a described situation, then a description of a test (back) cross.
findings.wentWrong: Some started from the wrong parental genotype so everything after it was wrong; only the more able could describe a test cross.
findings.rule: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner: any recessive offspring proves the unknown parent is heterozygous.

findings.asked: State the genotype terms for given allele pairs, draw a Punnett square and give a percentage.
findings.wentWrong: Surprisingly few could write 'homozygous dominant' and 'homozygous recessive'; the square itself was mostly right (three of four marks common) and 50% was often found.
findings.rule: Homozygous = two identical alleles (dominant or recessive); heterozygous = one of each.

findings.asked: Parental genotypes and alleles, then choose the correct Punnett squares from options.
findings.wentWrong: Genotypes were given by quite a few but the alleles by fewer; the unfamiliar 'choose the square' format was managed only by the better candidates.
findings.rule: An allele is one letter; a genotype is the pair.

insight.ruleToRemember: Write the parents' genotypes first (obey the bold words), then their gametes, then the square, then count the ratio or percentage the question asks for. Homozygous = two identical alleles, heterozygous = different; a test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner.
insight.aStarSignal: Correct genotypes from a pedigree with the reasoning stated, then a test cross explained in terms of what the offspring would reveal.
